overview: This unit covers Java methods (Methoden), parameters, and return values, as well as passing arrays. Java always copies the argument value when calling a method; for arrays, that value is the reference, so changes to elements can be visible. Insertion sort creates a sorted copy by inserting values one at a time into a sorted prefix. The order of the conditions ensures valid array access, the insertion position preserves stability, and the presented variant takes quadratic time.

entries.short: A method is a named, reusable block of code that encapsulates a task.
entries.explanation: A method groups statements under a name so they can be called and reused as needed. Methods help break a problem into smaller tasks. They can accept input values and return a value, or, as `void` methods, produce no result.
entries.example: A method such as `min` can find the smallest value in an array.
pitfalls: A method runs only when it is called.
entries.heading: 1. Methoden

entries.short: A method definition specifies, among other things, the return type, name, parameters, and body.
entries.explanation: In `public static int[] readArray(int number) { ... return result; }`, `public` and `static` indicate visibility and invocation type, `int[]` is the return type, and `readArray` is the method name. The parameters appear in parentheses, and the body contains the statements. A `return` statement ends the call and, for a method with a return type, provides the specified value.
entries.example: `int min(int[] b) { ... return result; }` defines a method that accepts an array and returns an `int`.
pitfalls: The return type describes the type of the returned value.
related: Formal parameter and actual argument (Formaler Parameter und aktuelles Argument)
entries.heading: Aufbau

entries.term: Formal parameter and actual argument (Formaler Parameter und aktuelles Argument)
entries.short: The formal parameter appears in the method definition; the actual argument is the specific value supplied when the method is called.
entries.explanation: A formal parameter is a variable through which a method receives an input value, such as `int[] b` in `min(int[] b)`. The actual argument is the value the caller supplies when calling the method, such as `a` in `min(a)`. When the method is called, the argument value is copied into the parameter.
entries.example: In `min(a)`, `b` is the formal parameter and `a` is the actual argument.
pitfalls: Parameters and arguments refer to different places in the program.
related: Copying values when calling a method (Wertkopie beim Methodenaufruf)
entries.heading: Begriffe

entries.short: A local variable exists only within the block in which it is declared.
entries.explanation: A local variable is declared inside a method or another block and is available there. Local variables with the same name in different methods are independent of one another. Therefore, `result` in `main` and `result` in `min` are two different variables.
entries.example: In `int result = min(a);`, `result` in `main` is initialized with the return value only after `min` returns.
pitfalls: Having the same name does not mean that two variables refer to the same memory location.
entries.heading: Begriffe

entries.term: void method and procedure (void-Methode und Prozedur)
entries.short: A `void` method returns no value and is also called a procedure.
entries.explanation: The return type `void` indicates that a method call produces no result. Such a method can still execute statements, for example changing an array or producing output. It finishes execution without returning a value.
entries.example: `public static void setFirst(int[] b) { b[0] = 9; }` is a `void` method.
pitfalls: `void` does not mean that the method has no effect.
related: Array mutation and reassignment (Mutation eines Arrays und Neuzuweisung)
entries.heading: Begriffe

entries.short: A precondition must be met for a method to be called correctly.
entries.explanation: The precondition describes what requirements the input must meet for the method to perform its task. The method `min` reads `b[0]` at the start, so the array passed to it must contain at least one element. Accessing this element in an empty array would be invalid.
entries.example: For `min(b)`, `b.length > 0` must hold.
pitfalls: A precondition is not automatically guaranteed by the method name.
entries.heading: Begriffe

entries.term: main and command-line arguments (main und Kommandozeilenargumente)
entries.short: `main(String[] args)` is the program's entry point, and the words after the class name are stored as strings in `args`.
entries.explanation: Java starts the program in the appropriate `main` method. The words supplied when the program starts appear as elements in the `args` array, starting at index `0`. Each element is a string and must be converted to another data type if needed.
entries.example: When started with `java Test Hel lo World!`, `args[0]`, `args[1]`, and `args[2]` contain the strings `"Hel"`, `"lo"`, and `"World!"`.
pitfalls: The class name itself is not an element of `args`.
entries.heading: und Kommandozeilenargumente

entries.short: A control-flow diagram represents program execution as nodes and directed arrows.
entries.explanation: Nodes can represent statements, decisions, the start, and the end; arrows show which steps may follow one another. Each method can be represented as its own subdiagram. A method call can appear as a separate node connected to the flow of the called method.
entries.example: In the diagram for `min`, a true loop test leads to the comparison `b[i] < result`; a false test ends the loop.
pitfalls: A method call is not the same as the entire control flow of the method being called.
related: Path and operational semantics (Pfad und operationale Semantik)
entries.heading: Kontrollflussdiagramm

entries.short: At a call, the called method executes; at return, execution resumes at the waiting call with the method's result.
entries.explanation: At a call, execution in the caller pauses and the called method begins with its own local variables. When it reaches `return`, that call ends and execution continues after the call site. With `int result = min(a);`, `result` is initialized only after the method returns.
entries.example: If `min(a)` returns the value `2`, then `result` in `main` becomes `2`, and `write(result)` is executed.
pitfalls: The caller executes the statement after the call only once the method call has finished.
entries.heading: Call und Return für

entries.term: Copying values when calling a method (Wertkopie beim Methodenaufruf)
entries.short: Java always passes arguments by copying their values.
entries.explanation: When a method is called, each formal parameter receives a copy of the actual argument's value. For a primitive type, this is the primitive value; for an array, it is the array reference value. Therefore, the method cannot reassign the caller's variable by changing its parameter.
entries.example: After `int n = 2; zero(n);`, `n` remains equal to `2`, even if `zero` sets the parameter `number` to `0`.
pitfalls: For arrays too, the reference is copied; the caller's variable itself is not passed.
related: Formal parameter and actual argument (Formaler Parameter und aktuelles Argument)
entries.heading: Basistyp: Die Methode bekommt eine Kopie

entries.short: A primitive type stores a primitive value, such as an integer, directly in a variable.
entries.explanation: When a primitive type is passed, its primitive value is copied into the formal parameter. A later assignment to the parameter therefore does not change the caller's variable. `int` is an example of a primitive type.
entries.example: In `int n = 2; zero(n);`, `number = 0` in `zero` does not change the variable `n`.
pitfalls: Changing the parameter value does not change the caller's variable.
related: Copying values when calling a method (Wertkopie beim Methodenaufruf)
entries.heading: Basistyp: Die Methode bekommt eine Kopie

entries.short: An array reference is the value a program uses to access an array.
entries.explanation: A variable of type `int[]` contains a reference to an array, not the array's elements themselves. If this reference is copied, the original variable and the copy can access the same array. Changes to elements can therefore be visible through both variables.
entries.example: After `int[] b = a;`, `a` and `b` refer to the same array.
pitfalls: Copying an array reference does not create a new array.
related: Copying values when calling a method (Wertkopie beim Methodenaufruf)
entries.heading: Übersicht

entries.term: Array mutation and reassignment (Mutation eines Arrays und Neuzuweisung)
entries.short: Changing an element affects the shared array, while reassigning the parameter changes only its local copy of the reference.
entries.explanation: If `b` and `a` refer to the same array, `b[0] = 9` changes the array that is also accessible through `a`. By contrast, `b = new int[2]` changes only what the local variable `b` refers to. The caller's variable `a` still points to the original array.
entries.example: `setFirst(a)` with `b[0] = 9` changes `a[0]`; `replace(a)` with `b = new int[2]` leaves `a` unchanged.
pitfalls: Assigning to a parameter does not reassign the caller's variable.
entries.heading: Übersicht

entries.short: Aliasing occurs when multiple variables refer to the same array.
entries.explanation: With aliasing, two or more variables access the same array. A change to an element through one of these variables is therefore also visible when accessing it through the others. This results from sharing references.
entries.example: After `int[] b = a;`, an assignment such as `b[0] = 9` is also visible through `a[0]`.
pitfalls: Two variables with the same contents do not necessarily point to the same array.
related: Array mutation and reassignment (Mutation eines Arrays und Neuzuweisung)
entries.heading: Übersicht

entries.short: A true array copy is made by creating a new array and copying each element into it.
entries.explanation: First create a new array with the same length as the original. Then copy each element from the original into the same index in the new array and return a reference to the new array. The new array is independent of the original, so changing its elements does not change the original.
entries.example: For `a = {7, 2}`, `copy(a)` creates a new array `{7, 2}`; then `b[0] = 9` can be executed without changing `a[0]`.
pitfalls: `int[] b = a` copies only the reference, not the array.
related: Array mutation and reassignment (Mutation eines Arrays und Neuzuweisung)
entries.heading: Echte Kopie erstellen

entries.short: Insertion sort sorts values by inserting each input value into an already sorted prefix.
entries.explanation: The method shown creates a new array `b` with the same length as the input `a`. It traverses the input from left to right and, for each index `i`, inserts the value `a[i]` into `b[0..i]` at its sorted position. Finally, it returns `b`, leaving the input unchanged and producing a sorted copy.
pitfalls: The implementation shown in the lecture searches for the insertion position from left to right.
related: Inserting into a sorted prefix (Einfügen in ein sortiertes Präfix)
entries.heading: 4. Insertion Sort

entries.short: A sorted prefix is the leading, already ordered part of an array.
entries.explanation: As insertion sort processes the input, `b[0..i-1]` contains the values processed so far in sorted order before `a[i]` is inserted. After the insertion, `b[0..i]` is sorted. The prefix therefore grows by one element in each iteration.
entries.example: Before the next value is inserted into `{1, 3, 7, 9}`, this array is the sorted prefix.
pitfalls: The prefix refers only to the already processed leading elements, not necessarily the entire array.
entries.heading: Zerlegung in Teilprobleme

entries.term: Insertion into a sorted prefix (Einfügen in ein sortiertes Präfix)
entries.short: An insertion finds the new value's position, shifts the following values to the right, and writes the value into the vacant position.
entries.explanation: Use `locate` to determine the insertion position `j` for `x` in the sorted prefix `b[0..i-1]`. Use `shift` to shift the values `b[j..i-1]` one position to the right. Then write `x` to `b[j]`; this way, `b[0..i]` contains the same values as before, plus `x`, in sorted order.
entries.example: When inserting `5` into `{1, 3, 7, 9}`, `j = 2`; after shifting and writing the value, the result is `{1, 3, 5, 7, 9}`.
pitfalls: The value must be written to `b[j]` only after the shift.
entries.heading: Ablauf einer Einfügung

entries.short: `locate` searches the sorted prefix for the insertion position of a new value.
entries.explanation: The method starts with `j = 0` and increments `j` while `j < i` and `x >= b[j]` hold. It then returns `j`. This is the first position where the new value can go before an existing larger value; with equal values, the search moves past them.
entries.example: For `b = {1, 3, 7, 9}`, `x = 5`, and `i = 4`, `locate` returns index `2`.
pitfalls: The search range ends exclusively at `i`.
related: Insertion into a sorted prefix (Einfügen in ein sortiertes Präfix)
entries.heading: Code

entries.short: `shift` shifts the values in `b[j..i-1]` one position to the right.
entries.explanation: Set `k` to `i - 1`. While `k >= j` holds, copy `b[k]` to `b[k + 1]` and decrement `k`. This frees position `j`, where the new value can then be written.
entries.example: With `j = 2` and `i = 4`, first `b[3]` is copied to `b[4]`, then `b[2]` is copied to `b[3]`.
pitfalls: The loop must also process `k = j` to free the insertion position.
related: Insertion into a sorted prefix (Einfügen in ein sortiertes Präfix)
Why shift proceeds from right to left (Warum shift von rechts nach links läuft)
entries.heading: Code

entries.term: Why shift proceeds from right to left (Warum shift von rechts nach links läuft)
entries.short: Shifting from right to left copies each value before its original position is overwritten.
entries.explanation: When shifting to the right, the source and destination ranges overlap. Starting on the right copies the last needed value to its destination first, before that destination overwrites another needed value. Shifting from left to right could cause values to be lost before they are copied.
entries.example: To shift `7` and `9` in `{1, 3, 7, 9, 0}` one position, first copy `9` from index `3` to `4`, then `7` from `2` to `3`.
pitfalls: Copying from left to right can destroy source data when ranges overlap.
related: Insertion into a sorted prefix (Einfügen in ein sortiertes Präfix)
entries.heading: Warum von rechts nach links schieben?

entries.short: With `&&`, the right operand is not evaluated if the left operand is false.
entries.explanation: In `j < i && x >= b[j]`, `j < i` is checked first. If `j < i` is false, the comparison with `b[j]` is skipped. In particular, when `j = i`, `b[i]` is not read.
entries.example: For `j = i`, `j < i` is false, so `x >= b[j]` is not evaluated.
pitfalls: If the conditions were reversed, `b[j]` could be read before the index check.
entries.heading: Short-Circuit bei

entries.short: A sorting algorithm is stable if elements with equal keys retain their original relative order.
entries.explanation: `locate` uses `x >= b[j]`, so it moves past equal values that have already been inserted. The new value of equal size is inserted after them. Thus, elements with equal sort keys retain their input order.
entries.example: When sorting people by age, a stable algorithm preserves the original order of two people who are the same age.
pitfalls: If `x >= b[j]` is replaced with `x > b[j]`, the new equal value may end up before the existing ones.
entries.heading: Stabilität durch

entries.short: The insertion-sort variant presented requires a quadratic number of steps in the number of elements.
entries.explanation: In iteration `i`, `locate` takes approximately `j` steps and `shift` takes exactly `i - j` copying steps; together, that is approximately `i` steps. Across all insertions, the total is $$\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} i = 1 + 2 + \dots + (n-1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \in \Theta(n^2).$$ Quadratic growth means that, for large `n`, doubling the input size takes approximately four times as much work.
pitfalls: The formula estimates the work; it is not an exact count of every machine operation.
entries.heading: 6. Kosten

entries.term: Call overhead and inlining (Call Overhead und Inlining)
entries.short: Helper methods organize code, and the JVM can reduce call costs through inlining.
entries.explanation: Breaking code into small methods such as `locate` and `shift` makes individual tasks clearer. A method call can add extra work, called call overhead. The JVM can replace a call with the method body; this optimization is called inlining.
entries.example: Where appropriate, the JVM can replace a call to `locate(b, x, i)` directly with the code of `locate`.
pitfalls: Inlining is a JVM optimization and does not change the program's meaning.
entries.heading: Helfer oder alles in einer Methode?

entries.short: An invariant is a statement that holds at a specified point in every iteration.
entries.explanation: For insertion sort, the central invariant after insertion in iteration `i` is: `b[0..i]` is sorted and contains exactly the first `i + 1` input values. It describes both the ordering of the values and the fact that no processed input value is lost or added. The invariant helps establish the algorithm's correctness.
entries.example: After inserting `a[2]`, `b[0..2]` is sorted and contains exactly `a[0]`, `a[1]`, and `a[2]`.
pitfalls: Sorted order alone is not enough; the invariant must also specify which values are present.
entries.heading: 7. Korrektheit

entries.term: Correctness of insertion sort (Korrektheit von Insertion Sort)
entries.short: After the final iteration, the result array is a sorted copy of the input.
entries.explanation: Before the first insertion, the empty prefix is sorted. In each iteration, the algorithm inserts the next input value at the position found and shifts existing values without losing them; thus, the invariant continues to hold for the longer prefix. When `i = n - 1`, the prefix covers the entire result array, which is therefore sorted and contains exactly the input values.
entries.example: For the input `{3, 1, 2}`, `sort` returns a new array `{1, 2, 3}`.
pitfalls: A correctly sorted result must also contain the same values as the input.
entries.heading: 7. Korrektheit
